The 10-year is -3bp since the hike vs a +22bp campaign average at the same point. The 2s10s steepening may be topping (intraday 3 of 4 signals: topping likely).

Up the stack: Nvidia 141bp, Oracle 305bp. Neocloud stocks 1m: CRWV -40%, NBIS -36%, IREN -39% vs NVDA -22%.

The biggest story of the session was rates. The US 2Y rose 17.6bp to 4.7377% and the 10Y rose 10.8bp to 4.9896%; the 30Y reached 5.3524% and the Gilt 10Y 5.223%. Higher yields hit long-duration tech again: the Nasdaq Composite fell -0.74% to 25065.88, the S&P 500 -0.38% to 7520.93 and the Russell 2000 -0.68%. US Info Tech fell -1.4% on the day and is down -12.61% over 1m. Overseas the tone was firmer: the Nikkei rose +2.87% to 60459.58 and the Euro Stoxx 50 +0.59%. Sentiment is mixed rather than panicked. The VIX fell 0.46 to 19.46 even as stocks fell, while the AAII bull-bear spread is -14.3, so retail investors are already bearish. AI credit: CoreWeave 5Y CDS is 1,221.7bp, 27.2bp above the 1,194.5bp Oct 15 record. It has given back 769.7bp of ground since the 452bp June low, so 103.7% of the original run is still in place. It eased -48.3bp on the day but is +68.2bp on the week. The stress is not spreading to the guarantor: Nvidia 5Y CDS is 140.69bp (-2.87bp on the day, -4.96bp on the week), and Microsoft (52.97bp), Meta (112.51bp) and Amazon (98.90bp) all tightened on the week. So far CDS buyers appear to accept Nvidia's backstop of the neoclouds. Nvidia equity tells a less comfortable story: -11.58% on the week, -22.07% on the month, and its DRSK model-implied CDS sits at the 100th percentile of its 1-year range. This is descriptive, not a validated signal. HY contagion: the Caa-B gap is 772bp, at the 99.2nd percentile of 5 years against a 419bp average. It has widened +203bp in 3m and Caa OAS is the widest since 2020-04-16. Is the CCC stress spreading? Partly, and slowly. Single-B is +18bp over 1m and +49bp over 3m, Ba +12bp and +44bp, and IG +8bp over 1m. All three tightened on the week (B -22bp, Ba -7bp, IG -3bp). The 63-day Caa/B correlation has risen to 0.66 from 0.35 three months ago, close to its 0.69 5-year median. That suggests CCC and single-B are starting to move together again; it is descriptive, not a signal. Tech analog: the phase model keeps the basket in Phase 1 (initial drop, credit calm), 25 days after the Oct 6 peak. The basket is down -18.01%, versus -16.25% for the 2000 basket at the same point. Three signposts are triggered: CoreWeave CDS is above its record, 64.29% of basket names are more than 20% off their highs (trigger 50%), and the SOX is -31.68% from its 52-week high (trigger -30%). The model's 6m odds of reaching P2 or P3 rose only 1.0pp from the prior session.

NY Harbor ULSD (US Diesel) — current: 413.09 cents/gal vs WTI

NY Harbor ULSD is at an extreme: the front month at 413.09 cents/gal sits at the 98.8th percentile, and all five gauges (outright, crack and the three curve spreads) are flagged high and at an extreme together. The squeeze is concentrated at the front of the curve. The curve is in steep backwardation, falling from 413.09 to 334.7 by the 12th month and 256.97 by the 36th, and the crack spread at 87.4578 $/bbl is the most stretched reading on the board (z 4.48). That points to acute prompt tightness in diesel rather than a broad repricing of crude. Past episodes like this have tended to unwind from the front, so every card leans SELL. The stops are very wide, though, which shows how violent these extremes can get before they mean-revert.

Two-sided analog episodes per signal: days where the signal's percentile-rank (vs its own full history) was <=5th or >=95th, or |z-score|>=1.3, clustered into one episode per zone per >=6-month gap between episode starts. For each zone, the realized forward 6-month % change in the BENCHMARK'S OUTRIGHT PRICE from each episode start is measured; a card's direction (BUY/SELL) is whichever sign that median historical move carries. Entry/target/stretch/stop are computed directly from this table -- the narrative prose (thesis/rationale) is the only part supplied by an LLM, and it is not permitted to alter a number. Crack spreads and curve shapes are, financially, relative-value signals rather than clean predictors of outright price; expressing every card in outright price terms is a deliberate simplification. HO36 Comdty (ULSD's 36-month point) is thin/less liquid on this seat -- treat its curve-shape reading with lower confidence than the others. Not investment advice.

Churn = the longest window of 20-120 sessions whose close range is <= 8x its median ATR(14), with median ADX(14) < 20, an insignificant close-price slope (p > 0.05), and >= 2 entries into each edge zone (top/bottom 20% of the band). Support/resistance = median swing low/high (+/-5 sessions); outer edges = the window's extreme closes. Breakout = a close beyond the outer edge by > 0.5 ATR, confirmed by a second close or one close beyond 1 ATR. A break back inside within 5 sessions is a failed break. An episode's outer edges can widen at most 0.5 ATR past their first detection, so a slow grind can't drag the range along with it. Base rates come from replaying the same rules over the full history, day by day, with no lookahead. This is pattern analysis of historical prices, not investment advice.

💧Treasury liquidity & rates volcomputed

US Govt Securities Liquidity Index (GVLQUSD), MOVE, Fed DKW term premium and TLT option skew, live from Bloomberg + federalreserve.gov.

Five charts tracking the mechanism Simon White laid out for why Treasury liquidity is deteriorating: rising inflation volatility feeds into a higher term premium, which steepens the curve, which raises bond vol, which shows up as worse UST market liquidity. Right now UST liquidity is at the 50th percentile of its own history (higher = worse) and the Fed's own DKW real term premium is +79bp.

Latest reading is +0.53 vol points (23th percentile of the 65 runs recorded so far). Positive means the 5%-OTM put is pricier than the at-the-money option -- the market paying up for downside-price / higher-yield insurance on long-end Treasuries.

UST liquidity index is 1.53 (50th percentile of its own 2007-present history -- 100th = worst liquidity on record), improving over the past 3 months (-0.08 pts). CPI YoY volatility (2yr) is 0.50pp; the article's thesis is that rising inflation vol drags liquidity worse, which this chart is built to let you check month to month.

Real term premium is +79bp (90th percentile of its own 2007-present history), up 1bp over the trailing ~2 months. Inflation risk premium is +11bp. Fed staff's own DKW decomposition (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei) splits the rise in long yields into a policy-uncertainty component (real term premium) and an inflation-uncertainty component -- both rising is the article's read that this move isn't just a rate-expectations story.

MOVE is 92.4 (66th percentile of its own post-2007 history). The 3m10s curve is 76bp (flatter by 12bp over 3 months). The article's claim is mechanical, not just correlated -- a steeper curve gives forward rates more room to move before converging to spot, which is itself higher realized/implied vol.

MOVE and the UST liquidity index have moved together with a full-history correlation of +0.72 (both series read as 'worse' when they rise). That's the closing link in the article's chain: inflation vol -> term premium -> curve steepness -> bond vol -> liquidity.

Recreates 5 charts from Bloomberg MacroScope, 'Treasury Market Liquidity Is a Live Issue Again' (Simon White, 19-Aug-2026). TLT skew accumulates one point per report run -- Bloomberg's option-surface field is snapshot-only, not retrievable historically via the API. Term premium is the Fed's own DKW model series (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei), pulled directly from federalreserve.gov, not Bloomberg. Not a trading signal -- a liquidity/vol monitor only.

No cup inside the window when its left rim is not the highest close of the 91 days before it, i.e. yields were already falling into the window. Pass level = cup base + 0.90 × (left rim − cup base).

🗞️Street View — Where the Cycle Is HeadingCURATED · AS OF 2026-10-01

⚠ Commentary is 40 days old (as of 2026-10-01); it may not reflect the latest Fed news.

Consensus is a short, shallow campaign: one or two more 25bp hikes, December more likely than October. The debate is whether hiking into an energy shock ends in recession, and the bond market is already doing some of the tightening.

The Fed

  • Sept 16: unanimous 25bp hike to 3.75–4.00%, the first since 2023. Dots: median one more hike in 2026; 16 of 18 see at least one, 4 see two. Inflation not back at 2% until 2029. (CNBC, FedAndMarkets)
  • Warsh's message was distinctly hawkish (inflation 'too high and broad-based'); the Conference Board calls it 'not a one and done'. (Conference Board)
  • Sept 29, Williams (NY Fed): 'no need for urgency'; one more hike 'late this year' may be appropriate; the biggest inflation shocks have passed. (Bloomberg, NY Fed)
  • Sept 30, August PCE came in soft: headline 3.4% (vs 3.7% expected), core 3.0% (vs 3.3%). October odds fell; December still priced. Kashkari: inflation 'still too high'. (CNBC, CNBC (Kashkari))

Market pricing

  • October 28 hike odds vary widely by venue, roughly 35% to 69% (prediction markets highest, CME futures ~58%), mostly measured before the soft PCE print. (PredictionMarketsPicks)
  • About 83% odds of another hike by year-end; futures price ~93bp of tightening over the next 9 meetings, more than the dots. (Forbes)

Bonds and credit

  • 10-year Treasury above 5.25% (Sept 28), the highest since 2007; 30-year ~5.49%. Drivers cited: sticky energy inflation (Iran war), heavy issuance, AI capex demand. Term premium ~1.0–1.4%. (CNBC, CNBC (Warsh's yield problem))
  • AI-related issuers trade ~115bp vs ~78bp for IG overall; high-yield AI supply $40B year to date vs $12B in all of 2025. BNP and Goldman warn the issuance could pressure spreads. (Reuters, Bloomberg (BNP))

The bear case

  • Rosenberg: the Fed has never hiked into an energy shock without a recession, and AI won't save it this time. (TheStreet)
  • Goldman called the case for hiking 'weak' (demand not overheating, energy inflation should fade when the war ends). Oxford Economics: 'The Fed cannot control energy prices'; the risk is a weaker labor market. (CNN)

Read-through: For bonds, the bigger risk is the long end, not the Fed: term premium and supply keeping the 10-year above 5% matter more than one extra 25bp. The recession call is loud but isn't in any sell-side house view yet.

Curated summary of published Fed, market and economist commentary (news and research via the web), not a computed series and not a forecast. Odds differ by venue and move daily.

🔥Is Inflation Persistent?

Persistence score: 64/100 — Persistent. Underlying inflation is sticky and broad, but not accelerating sharply. Core PCE is 3.12% and core CPI 2.6%. The trimmed and median measures cluster from 2.26% to 2.89%, and Median CPI and Trimmed-Mean CPI are both trending up. The computed Core-Trend Sub-Score is shown separately and points the same way: underlying measures sit in the upper part of their history. The Dallas distribution shows breadth: 52.6% of the PCE basket is inflating above 3% (16.6% above 10%), while only 25.6% is falling. Markets are not pricing persistence: the 1y breakeven is 1.9922% and the 5y 2.2595%. That leaves room for an upside repricing of front-end yields, consistent with today's 17.6bp jump in the 2Y.

🫧Tech Bubble Peak Again?vs March 2000
BUBBLE RESEMBLANCE · SUPER COUNT computed
9 of 22 indicators at peak-like levels · 7 beyond 2000 — 59/100
Today looks like early bust, not the March-2000 peak. Equity froth has already deflated well short of 2000 levels. Nasdaq trailing P/E is 38.84x, 15% of the way to 2000 peak conditions. The Nasdaq is -0.2% versus its 200DMA (0% of the way to peak stretch), and SOX P/E 33.75x is 34%. The late-cycle catalysts are mixed. Credit is complacent: IG tightness is 126% and Baa-10Y 156% of the 2000 peak condition, and the NFCI shows loose financial conditions at 148%. But the curve is positive (2s10s +25.19bp) and the PMIs (55.5 manufacturing, 54.5 services) are not rolling over. Sentiment signposts are washed out: AAII is -14.3 (14%) and consumer confidence 91.7 (31%). The phase model places the tech basket in Phase 1 (initial drop, credit calm). Over 6m it puts Phase 1 at 0.574, Phase 2 at 0.202, Phase 3 at 0.102 and Phase 4 at 0.122. It puts the chance of ever reaching Phase 2 or worse at 0.37 within 6m and 0.541 within 12m. Those are model estimates, not certainties. The basket is down -18.01% versus -16.25% for 2000 at the same point, so the drawdown is tracking slightly ahead of the 2000 path.

Bubble-analog — today's Nasdaq vs the dot-com cycle (two anchors)

WHY TWO START DATES?
Each line is rebased to 100 at a low the tech bull launched from, so elapsed time lines up. Oct-2022 is today's anchor — it was the prior bear-market bottom. Oct-1990 is the dot-com cycle's equivalent (its literal prior bear bottom). But 1990 predates the internet mania by ~4 years, so the second chart re-anchors the dot-com line to the 1994 reset low, just before the surge ignited, for a tighter like-for-like. Today sits very early under the strict 1990 analog, further along under the 1994 surge analog.
━ Anchored at the prior bear-market bottom (Oct-1990)   ━ today's cycle
━ Anchored at the pre-internet reset low (1994)   ━ today's cycle

Valuation marker: today's Nasdaq P/E (39x) ≈ 22% of the ~175x 2000-peak P/E.

IF THIS RHYMES WITH 2000
Nasdaq fell -78.0% peak→trough (2000-03-10 → 2002-10-09, ~31 months); it took ~15 years to reclaim the high.

Three signposts are triggered. CoreWeave CDS is above its 1,194.5bp record, 64.29% of basket names are more than 20% off their highs, and the SOX is -31.68% from its 52-week high. In 2000, the shift from Phase 1 to Phase 2 came when the stress moved from equities into broad credit. Today HY OAS (326bp) is 122bp short of that trigger and Baa-10Y is moving away from its trigger. The regime models agree that credit is calm: credit calm 0.972, HMM Phase-1-like 0.999. The rally-watch shows a spike-and-turn in VIX, which sets up rally conditions. Credit calm is the one core condition that fails (+13bp versus +10bp or less). History warns that 45.5% of such rallies were traps (a typical +10.3% over 13 days), versus +29.6% over 83 days for the real ones. My own estimates (concentration, IPO froth, CAPE, market cap/GDP, LT EPS growth) are analyst estimates and were not verified by search this session. The Anthropic IPO (Renaissance estimates about $75bn) and SK hynix's $26.5bn listing support a high reading for IPO froth.

Odds the volatility-washout conditions line up within a week: 14%; within two weeks: 26%. Rallies of 8%+ that start in this phase: 46% later fail below their starting low (median 13 trading days, +10%); the rest become recoveries (median 83 days, +30%). Descriptive, not a signal.

Positioning tilt (generic, historical): Historically, at this phase mix the phase-conditional optimum has favoured gold, Treasury duration and investment-grade credit, over mega-cap growth, developed international and emerging markets.

Phases are rules with the same thresholds in 2000 and today: Phase 2 = HY OAS +150bp or Baa-10y +50bp from the basket's peak; Phase 3 = Sahm rule or ISM < 47 for 3 months AND bank stress (KBW -25% or C&I charge-offs >= 1% and rising); Phase 4 = basket +20% off its low, above its 200-day average, HY 150bp off its wide. Odds come from every Nasdaq-100 drop since 1985 that reached today's depth, weighted by how closely its credit, macro and volatility readings matched today's, plus a small labelled judgment overlay for AI-credit stress. 'Ever P2+' = chance spreads cross the Phase-2 line at any point before the horizon. Model estimates on ~40 episodes: read them to within +/-10 points. Not financial advice.

🏦Fed Chair Warsh
NEAR TERM

Next meeting: hold, with a hawkish tilt on the balance sheet. This is inferred. I could not verify the current target range or Warsh's confirmation status this session. The last range I could confirm was 3.5%-3.75%, after a spring meeting with two dissents for a cut. The 2Y at 4.7377% is well above that range, so markets price a higher path than that.

~1 YEAR

Inferred from his record: he presses for a smaller Fed balance sheet and less forward guidance. He is open to cuts, justified by AI-driven productivity, but only if sticky inflation (core PCE 3.12%) cooperates. A committee wary of inflation constrains him, since the chair has one vote.

Warsh was seen as the most hawkish finalist. He later argued that AI-driven productivity allows strong growth without inflation, which would make room for cuts. He inherits a board divided on cuts, and forecasts of slow disinflation 'don't support deep cuts.' Inference: his first moves are more likely to be balance-sheet and communications changes than rate cuts, especially with sticky core measures rising and front-end yields up 17.6bp today. I could not verify any speech or decision from November 2026; treat all of this as inference from prior statements.

Sources: Axios: Kevin Warsh's challenges become clear after Powell's last hurrah · Yahoo Finance: Kevin Warsh's Fed record - what it signals for interest rates · Trump's Fed chair nominee inherits divided board on rate cuts

Descriptive regime read, not advice and not a recommendation to trade. Rule results are simulations on one market history (3x daily returns rebuilt from index data, 1-day lag, costs), and the exits (+10% target, 5-day pause) were chosen after testing a few values on that same history, so treat them as in-sample. The trend+vol engine is a drawdown control, not proven timing skill (trendvol TRENDVOL.md § CORRECTION). Credit widening = 63-day change past the monitor_spread triggers (Baa +0.15pp, HY OAS +0.50pp, IG OAS +0.15pp); as a standalone overlay that rule failed its pre-registered gates. Leveraged and inverse ETFs reset daily and decay.
